description:
Found by writing the JSON scanner fz-5xp.17 needs, which is what surfaced it:
the natural Elixir spelling silently does nothing.

    fnp lit(<<"true", rest :: binary>>), do: {:true_lit, rest}
    fnp lit(bin), do: {:no, bin}

    lit("true,x")
      elixir  {:true_lit, ",x"}
      fz      {:no, "true,x"}      on interp, run and build

No error and no warning -- the clause simply never matches, so control falls to
the next one. A scanner written this way looks right, compiles, runs, and is
wrong.

A BYTE VALUE in the same position works:

    <<32, rest :: binary>>      matches a leading space
    <<" ", rest :: binary>>     does not
    <<" " :: binary, rest :: binary>>   does not either

So the bitstring pattern machinery is fine; it is specifically a STRING LITERAL
as a segment that fails, in both the bare and the `:: binary`-annotated forms.

WHY IT IS P1. Every JSON token is a literal: `true`, `false`, `null`, `{`, `}`,
`[`, `]`, `,`, `:`, `"`. Writing the decoder with byte values instead
(`<<34, rest :: binary>>` for a quote) is possible and is what the probe had to
do, but it turns a readable scanner into numeric soup and diverges from the
Elixir twin the oracle compares against -- the twin can use literals, so the
two programs stop being the same program.

DONE = a string literal segment in a bitstring pattern matches the bytes it
spells, on all three doors, with a fixture whose oracle is the same scanner in
Elixir. Check the empty literal and a literal with escapes while in there.

WATCH OUT: whatever decides this today does so SILENTLY. Whatever the fix, a
segment the matcher cannot honour should be a diagnostic rather than a clause
that never fires.
title: [BUG] A string literal in a bitstring pattern silently never matches
